narrative:
The model estimated a 61.9% probability that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That means failure was judged more likely than success, and under the law school’s risk policy this estimate led to denial. It is a probability, not a certainty, but it was high enough to drive the decision.

The strongest influence was your third-year class decile. Being in decile 3, compared with accepted students averaging near decile 6, was the largest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.50, above the accepted average of 3.23, was the main counterweight and pushed toward passing. Your LSAT score of 33, below the accepted average of about 37, was the next most important factor and also leaned toward failure.

To move forward, ask admissions for feedback and consider retaking the LSAT if you can reasonably improve it. Speak with academic advisors about your third-year record and build concrete evidence of bar-exam readiness, such as a structured prep plan or additional coursework. If you reapply or appeal, include updated scores and a clear plan showing how you will address the factors that raised concern.
